inline.s: [Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Tang dynasty, by imperial decree]
Xuanzang, the Tripitaka Master of the Tang dynasty, translated this sutra by imperial command.

[Tripitaka Master] “Tripitaka” refers to the canon of sutras, the canon of vinaya, and the canon of treatises. The canon of sutras is the scriptures spoken by the Buddha; the canon of vinaya is the precepts laid down by the Buddha; the canon of treatises is the treatises composed by the Buddha’s disciples. A “Tripitaka Master” is a bhiksu who has mastered all three canons—sutra, vinaya, and treatise. [Xuanzang] Great Master Xuanzang (602–664), a celebrated Tripitaka Master of the Tang dynasty, is honored together with Kumarajiva and Paramartha as one of China’s three great translators of Buddhism, and he was one of the founders of the Consciousness-Only school. [Translated by imperial decree] Great Master Xuanzang translated this sutra by command of Emperor Taizong of the Tang.

Great Master Xuanzang was born in the second year of the Renshou era of the Sui dynasty. As a child he followed his second elder brother, Master Changjie, and lived at the Jingtu monastery in Luoyang, where he studied the Dharma. At eleven (in 613) he had already memorized the Lotus Sutra and the Vimalakirti Sutra. At thirteen (in 615), when the monastic ordination examination was held in Luoyang, his excellent performance won him exceptional selection despite his youth. Thereafter he listened to Master Jing lecture on the Nirvana Sutra, studied the Mahayanasamgraha with Master Yan, ascended the seat to repeat the teaching, and analyzed it so thoroughly that he won the admiration of the assembly.

[Ordination by examination] In ancient times, the court established a system for ordaining monks, in order to control the number of monks and nuns and to guarantee their quality, and it was forbidden to leave the household life privately. It was stipulated that one who wished to leave the household life had first to pass an examination on the Buddhist scriptures before being permitted to receive the tonsure.

Later, Great Master Xuanzang traveled on to study in various places and quickly exhausted the doctrines of every school; his talent was praised on all sides and his fame filled the capital. The minister Xiao Yu presented a memorial requesting that he be made to reside at the Zhuangyan monastery. Because he felt deeply that the teachings he had heard during many years of seeking the Dharma in various regions were inconsistent with one another—especially the theories concerning dharma characteristics held by the then-popular Shelun school (later absorbed into the Faxiang school) and the Dilun school, which often contradicted each other—he longed to obtain the Yogacarabhumi Sastra, which comprehensively encompasses the teachings of the three vehicles, in order to merge and penetrate everything. He therefore resolved to journey to India in search of the Dharma.

Because he could not obtain the travel document (passport) issued by the Tang court, his wish was never fulfilled. In 627, at the age of twenty-five, Great Master Xuanzang resolutely set out from Chang’an on his own, braving the journey to India (today’s India). Under exceptionally perilous and harsh conditions, with indomitable heroic spirit he overcame layer upon layer of hardship and obstacle and finally reached India.

During the more than ten years he spent in India, Great Master Xuanzang studied with and consulted many eminent masters. Among the monasteries where he stayed was Nalanda monastery, the celebrated Buddhist center then at the height of its fame. There he studied the Yogacarabhumi Sastra and other sutras and treatises with the abbot, the master of Indian Buddhist learning, the scholar-monk Silabhadra. Silabhadra was a disciple of Dharmapala and a second-generation disciple of Bodhisattva Vasubandhu. In the thirteenth year of the Zhenguan era, Great Master Xuanzang, on behalf of Master Silabhadra, lectured at Nalanda on the Mahayanasamgraha and the Vijnaptimatratasiddhi Sastra. Thereafter, Xuanzang also traveled on foot to survey the whole of the South Asian subcontinent.

Great Master Xuanzang not only was deeply accomplished in the Dharma but was also fluent in Sanskrit, so he took part in religious debate assemblies again and again and won them all, his renown rising day by day. At the invitation of King Harsha he presided over the great unimpeded debate assembly on the meaning of the Dharma at Kanauj, extolling the Mahayana teaching. Those who gathered included the kings of eighteen kingdoms, more than three thousand monks of both the Greater and Lesser Vehicles, over two thousand Brahmins and exponents of non-Buddhist doctrines, and more than a thousand monks of Nalanda. The Master served as the chief disputant and instructed the assembly. He further declared: “If among my words there is a single one that is unreasonable and that someone can refute, I beg that my head be cut off in atonement.” Eighteen days passed, and in the end no one dared to come forward to dispute, so he won without a battle. When the assembly dispersed, everyone rejoiced, exclaiming that they had never seen the like. Thus his name rose suddenly, and his authority shook all of India; by the Mahayana practitioners of his day he was hailed as Mahayanadeva (Heaven of the Great Vehicle), and by followers of the Lesser Vehicle as Mokshadeva (Heaven of Liberation), and King Harsha paid him homage as his teacher.

In 643, Great Master Xuanzang set out for home laden with honor, bringing back 657 Buddhist scriptures to the Central Land. In 645 he returned to Chang’an and was warmly received and consoled by Emperor Taizong. In 652, in the western courtyard of the Ci’en monastery within Chang’an, he built a five-story pagoda (the present-day Giant Wild Goose Pagoda) to store the scriptures and images he had brought back from India. In 1962 a memorial hall to Great Master Xuanzang was established within the monastery. The Giant Wild Goose Pagoda has become an architectural monument to Xuanzang’s westward quest for the Dharma and his translation of scriptures upon his return.

With the strong support of Emperor Taizong, Great Master Xuanzang established a scripture-translation institute (a national translation academy) in Chang’an, and the outstanding scholars who took part in the translation came from throughout the country and from the nations of East Asia. He spent more than ten years within Yuhua Palace translating many scriptures into Chinese. These Buddhist scriptures later spread from China to the Korean peninsula, Vietnam, and Japan.
By translating Buddhist texts and expounding the scriptures, Great Master Xuanzang founded the Chinese Faxiang Consciousness-Only school, and his doctrine deeply influenced many other schools.

The sutras and treatises the Master translated in his lifetime total seventy-four works, altogether 1,338 fascicles, including the six-hundred-fascicle Great Prajna Paramita Sutra—the most of any translator in the Central Land. Chinese Buddhism, through Great Master Xuanzang’s westward quest for the Dharma, which traced the matter to its very source, attained the complete essence of the Buddha’s teaching, and from then on flourished in China.

The Master passed away on the fifth day of the second month of the first year of the Linde era (5 February 664), and was buried on White Deer Plain. Tens of thousands of mourners attended the funeral; the emperor (Emperor Gaozong of the Tang) grieved and wept bitterly, and did not hold court for three days.

Profound Meaning” refers to setting forth, before the annotation of the text, the deep and subtle principle that this sutra expounds; this is the outline of the whole sutra. It leads the reader to grasp the general whole first and only then to study the text, so that the main points stand out and all is easy to comprehend and grasp.
The central idea (profound meaning) of this sutra is:
to leave illusion and emerge from the dream.
In the Mahaparinirvana Sutra
Chapter Forty, the Buddha said:
“All dharmas are all false and unreal.”

This means that all dharmas are illusory appearances, like the affairs of a dream. In fact, all sentient beings, sunk in the dream of ignorance, experience all kinds of suffering and hardship; therefore to leave illusion and emerge from the dream is the core of the Dharma, the true meaning of prajna paramita, and the essential point of the Heart Sutra.
In the Sutra of Complete Enlightenment, the Buddha said:

“All sentient beings, from time without beginning, have been in manifold inverted states, like a deluded person who shifts his direction again and again, falsely taking the four great elements as the mark of his own body and the shadow-images of the six sense objects as the mark of his own mind. Like one with diseased eyes who sees flowers in the sky and a second moon: in the sky there are in truth no flowers, yet the sick one grasps them falsely. Because of this false grasping, he is not merely deluded about the nature of empty space, but is also confused as to where the real flowers arise. Because of this false existence, he revolves in birth and death, and this is called ignorance. This ignorance has no real substance, like a person in a dream who, while dreaming, is not without something, yet upon waking finds nothing at all obtained. Like all the flowers in the sky, it vanishes into empty space and cannot be said to have a definite place of extinction. Why? Because there is no place of arising. All sentient beings, within the unborn, falsely see birth and death; therefore they are said to revolve in birth and death.”
(For the annotations, see
The Detailed Explanation of the Sutra of Complete Enlightenment
In the Surangama Sutra, the Buddha said:

“You should know that all sentient beings, from time without beginning, continue in birth and death, all because they do not know the ever-abiding true mind, that nature that is pure, bright, and clear
(all because they do not know the pure, bright, clear nature that abides in the true mind)
, and instead give rise to all manner of false thought
(and go on to employ false thought)
; this thought is not true, and so there is revolution.”
This sutra says:
“When the bodhisattva Avalokitesvara practiced the profound prajna paramita, he illuminated and saw that all five aggregates are empty, and passed beyond all suffering and calamity.”
This is the bodhisattva’s direct realization that body and mind are illusory appearances, and so he awakened and emerged from suffering. Again:

“Because nothing is attained, the bodhisattva, relying on prajna paramita, has no hindrance in mind. Without hindrance, there is no fear; far from inverted dream-thoughts, he reaches ultimate nirvana.”
and
“All Buddhas of the three times, relying on prajna paramita, attain anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.”
All speak of leaving illusion and emerging from the dream.
In
The Detailed Explanation of the Diamond Sutra
, there is a detailed discussion of the dream of ignorance and of how one leaves illusion.
Note: The headings in the text below have been added by the annotator and do not belong to the sutra itself.

blocks.text: 1. The Five Aggregates Are All Empty

inline.s: [When the bodhisattva Avalokitesvara practiced the profound prajna paramita, he illuminated and saw that all five aggregates are empty, and passed beyond all suffering and calamity.]

When the bodhisattva Avalokitesvara, cultivating the profound Dharma gate of wonderful wisdom that leaves illusion and realizes Buddhahood, in the samadhi of wisdom light illuminated and saw that body and mind are both illusory, he therefore passed calmly through all suffering and calamity.

Practice” is the wonderful wisdom that leaves illusion. “Profound” refers to the depth and degree of the practice. “Illuminate” means to contemplate with the light of wisdom inherent in one’s own nature.

Suffering is everywhere. And suffering arises from craving, and craving arises from clinging to the five aggregates of body and mind as “self.” So long as there is clinging to the five aggregates of body and mind, there is necessarily suffering; the deeper the clinging, the greater the suffering. Therefore it is said:
“illuminates and sees that all five aggregates are empty, and passes beyond all suffering and calamity.”

All sentient beings are endowed with the nature of awareness, luminous, clear, empty, and still, in no way different from the Buddha. But because, from kalpas without beginning, they have never awakened, they falsely cling to body and mind (form, feeling, thinking, conditioning, consciousness) as self (the mark of self), and so give rise to feelings of love and aversion, grasping and rejecting. Then, following their feelings, they create karma; following their karma, they receive retribution, and through birth, aging, sickness, and death they revolve through long kalpas.

[Avalokitesvara] “Isvara” means self-mastery—existing autonomously. Sentient beings, from kalpas without beginning, are pulled and turned by objective conditions and false thought, wandering through birth and death without self-mastery. Avalokitesvara means to break through the illusion of objective conditions and false thought, to achieve not turning with thoughts, not being pulled along by conditions, a mind without hindrance, and autonomous existence. Someone asked the Elder Master Guangqin: “Where should one begin in seated meditation?” The old master answered: “Begin with Avalokitesvara.” (See the essay “The Fruit-Monk Who Is Free Everywhere.”) [Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva] Another name of the Bodhisattva Guanyin. The Dharma has two levels: one is self-benefit—realizing the Buddha path; the other is benefiting others—delivering sentient beings. Avalokitesvara is named after self-benefit, and Guanyin is named after benefiting others. Master Kumarajiva’s translation of the Heart Sutra, the Mahaprajnaparamita Great Bright Mantra Sutra, says:
“The bodhisattva Avalokitesvara, when practicing the profound prajna paramita, illuminated and saw that the five aggregates are empty, and passed beyond all suffering and calamity.”

[The five aggregates] Also called the “five aggregates.” The five aggregates are the aggregates of form, feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness—the five great elements that constitute body and mind. Among them, the aggregate of form refers to matter and is called “dharma of form”; the four aggregates of feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness belong to the mental and are called “dharmas of mind.” The aggregate of form is the body; the other four aggregates (feeling, thinking, conditioning, consciousness) are the mind. Master Yinguang said:

“The five aggregates are form, feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness. Form is the body received as the retribution of karma; feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness are the illusory, deluded mind that arises upon contact with objects. Through these illusory dharmas of body and mind, in the realm of the six sense objects, one stirs up confusion and creates karma.”
(From the Essence of Master Yinguang’s Collected Writings.) The Nirvana Sutra says:

“At the moment of death, one’s kin and kindred weep. The person is terrified and cannot contain himself. The good and evil of a whole life all appear before his eyes. After the warmth is exhausted, the five aggregates of the past are extinguished, and the intermediate being of the present arises. After entering the womb, the intermediate being of the present is extinguished, and the five aggregates of the future arise. It is like a lamp being lit and darkness vanishing, and the lamp being extinguished and darkness returning—continuing without interruption.”
The Buddha Vipasyin said:

“Borrowing the four great elements to make a body, the mind is originally unborn but arises because of objects. If the objects before one are absent, the mind too is absent; guilt and merit, like illusion, arise and likewise vanish.”

(From the Compendium of the Five Lamps.) [The four great elements] The elements of earth, water, fire, and wind. Earth has hardness as its nature, water wetness as its nature, fire warmth as its nature, and wind movement as its nature. All tangible matter in the world possesses these four natures of hardness, wetness, warmth, and movement, and so they are called “great.” [If the objects before one are absent, the mind too is absent; guilt and merit, like illusion, arise and likewise vanish] Without objects there is no mind; without mind, guilt and merit vanish. Guilt is evil karma, merit is good karma; both are causes of the turning of birth and death. [The intermediate being] The intermediate being, also called the “intermediate existence” or “bardo,” is a transformation body formed of subtle matter that sustains life after death and before rebirth; this transformation body is the intermediate being. During the first forty-nine days, this intermediate being undergoes birth and death every seven days, passing through seven rounds of birth and death, awaiting the arrangement of karmic conditions, and then goes to take rebirth.
[Illuminates and sees that all five aggregates are empty] means to illuminate and see that all five aggregates are illusory. The Mahaprajnaparamita Sutra
Chapter Eleven, “The Study of Illusion,” says:

“Subhuti, what do you think? Is form different from illusion? Are feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness different from illusion? Subhuti replied: No, World-Honored One......Form is not different from illusion; illusion is not different from form; form is illusion, illusion is form. World-Honored One, feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness are not different from illusion; illusion is not different from feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness; consciousness is illusion, illusion is consciousness......The Buddha told Subhuti: What do you think? Does illusion have defilement and purity? No, World-Honored One. Subhuti, what do you think? Does illusion have arising and ceasing? No, World-Honored One.”
Read this chapter carefully, and you will know that “emptiness” in the Heart Sutra means “illusion.”

The root of all sentient beings, from time without beginning, sinking in the sea of suffering and revolving through the six paths of samsara is the false clinging to body and mind as real. In the Sutra of Complete Enlightenment, the Buddha said:

“All sentient beings, from time without beginning, have been in manifold inverted states, like a deluded person who shifts his direction again and again, falsely taking the four great elements as the mark of his own body and the shadow-images of the six sense objects as the mark of his own mind. Like one with diseased eyes who sees flowers in the sky and a second moon: in the sky there are in truth no flowers, yet the sick one grasps them falsely. Because of this false grasping, he is not merely deluded about the nature of empty space, but is also confused as to where the real flowers arise. Because of this false existence, he revolves in birth and death, and this is called ignorance. This ignorance has no real substance, like a person in a dream who, while dreaming, is not without something, yet upon waking finds nothing at all obtained. Like all the flowers in the sky, it vanishes into empty space and cannot be said to have a definite place of extinction. Why? Because there is no place of arising. All sentient beings, within the unborn, falsely see birth and death; therefore they are said to revolve in birth and death.”

Sentient beings create karma, receive retribution, and revolve precisely because they falsely cling to these five aggregates of body and mind as self! In the contemplation of the emptiness of the very self, this is what one should first look upon.

[Shadow-images of the six sense objects] The various thoughts that the six sense faculties produce by conditioning on the six sense objects; because these thoughts are all illusory and unreal, they are called the shadow-images of the six sense objects—the illusory reflections of conditioning on the six sense objects.
The Surangama Sutra says:

“You should know that all sentient beings, from time without beginning, continue in birth and death, all because they do not know the ever-abiding true mind, that nature that is pure, bright, and clear, and instead give rise to all manner of false thought; this thought is not true, and so there is revolution.”

(Translation: You should know that all sentient beings, from time without beginning, continue in birth and death all because they do not know that which abides in their own pure, bright, luminous nature, and instead employ false thought, taking body and mind as self, and so pursue objects and create karma; this false thought is not true, and so there is the turning of birth and death.)

[Passes beyond all suffering and calamity] Because all suffering and calamity are feelings of body and mind; once one awakens and directly realizes that body and mind are illusory, one no longer undergoes them. The Buddha said:

“Sariputra! Because form is empty, there is no mark of vexation and destruction; because feeling is empty, there is no mark of feeling; because thinking is empty, there is no mark of knowing; because conditioning is empty, there is no mark of doing; because consciousness is empty, there is no mark of perceiving.”
(From the Mahaprajnaparamita Sutra
Chapter Three, “Practice and Response.”) [Suffering and calamity] hardship and disaster.
If one clings to existence, then feelings arise and suffering arises; if one destroys existence, then feelings vanish and suffering is extinguished—passing beyond all suffering and calamity.
[Clinging to existence] Falsely clinging to body, mind, and the world as real existence.

In studying the Heart Sutra, one should first work on “not dwelling on objects and thus giving rise to mind,” and in daily life realize that all objects and conditions are illusory appearances—dreaming and experiencing within a dream. “As all things pass before the eyes, one distinguishes good and bad; in the end, none of it concerns one.” When the effort matures, the mind becomes settled, prajna arises of itself, and afflictions and karmic obstructions diminish day by day. Sometimes, if one is disturbed beyond endurance by past dust and former affairs, at once gather the mind in and respectfully recite the Heart Sutra, and the marks of karma will vanish of themselves.
Master Hanshan said:

“This one Prajna Sutra speaks solely of a single contemplation of emptiness, and so is the first gate of entry to the Great Vehicle and the wondrous method of bodhisattva practice. The Sanskrit word ‘prajna’ is here rendered as wisdom. Therefore, in benefiting living beings
(benefiting sentient beings)

, the bodhisattva takes wisdom as foremost. As it is said, ‘without wisdom, expedient means bind; with wisdom, expedient means liberate.’ Yet this contemplation of emptiness, though contained within the eight Prajna divisions, is in its essentials found only in the fourteen lines of the Heart Sutra, which already include
(include)

everything. The Heart Sutra, a single fascicle, in turn lies solely in the line ‘illuminates and sees that all five aggregates are empty,’ which already exhausts its meaning. And within this single line, if one begins to practice, it lies only in the one word ‘illuminate’—this is the simplest and most essential gateway.”
(From the Dream-Wandering Collection
The Rite of Transformation and Rebirth.)

[Expedient means] The means, methods, or language adopted to guide and teach sentient beings. “Expedient means” is spoken in contrast to “ultimate reality.” [Without wisdom, expedient means bind; with wisdom, expedient means liberate] Here expedient means refers to benefiting sentient beings through manifold skillful means. The meaning of “without wisdom, expedient means bind; with wisdom, expedient means liberate” is: abiding in illusion (without wisdom) to benefit sentient beings results in being bound; leaving illusion (with wisdom) to benefit sentient beings results in liberation and freedom. Therefore, the bodhisattva should benefit sentient beings with wisdom (“the bodhisattva, in benefiting living beings, takes wisdom as foremost”). Hence, in delivering sentient beings, the bodhisattva should say: I shall liberate immeasurable sentient beings to extinction, yet in truth there are no sentient beings who are liberated to extinction. (For details, see
The Detailed Explanation of the Diamond Sutra
[Liberating sentient beings to extinction] Liberating sentient beings to Buddhahood.
The Vimalakirti Sutra says:

“Without wisdom, expedient means bind; with wisdom, expedient means liberate......What is meant by ‘without wisdom, expedient means bind’? It is when a bodhisattva abides in the afflictions of greed, anger, and wrong views, and yet plants the roots of all virtue—this is called ‘without wisdom, expedient means bind.’ What is meant by ‘with wisdom, expedient means liberate’? It is when one, leaving the afflictions of greed, anger, and wrong views, plants the roots of all virtue and dedicates it to anuttara-samyak-sambodhi—this is called ‘with wisdom, expedient means liberate.’”

[Planting the roots of all virtue] Accumulating various merits by benefiting sentient beings. [The Rite of Transformation and Rebirth] The gradual rules of expedient means for delivering sentient beings.

blocks.text: 2. Form and Emptiness Are Not Two

inline.s: From here down to the end of the sutra, all is spoken by the bodhisattva Avalokitesvara.
[Sariputra! Form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is not different from form; form is emptiness, emptiness is form. Feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness are likewise so.]

The great being Guanyin said to Sariputra: Sariputra! He who wishes to study this profound prajna paramita Dharma gate should contemplate that the five aggregates are all empty: form (body) is not different from illusion, illusion is not different from form, form is illusion, illusion is form; feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness (mind) are likewise so.
In the Mahaprajnaparamita Sutra, Chapter Eleven, “The Study of Illusion,”

“the Buddha told Subhuti: ......Subhuti, what do you think? Is form different from illusion? Are feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness different from illusion? Subhuti replied: No, World-Honored One.”

[Sariputra] This is Sariputra, one of the Buddha’s ten great disciples, renowned as “foremost in wisdom.” “Sari” is the name of his mother, and “putra” is rendered into Chinese as “son.” Sariputra is a transliteration; in translating scriptures there is also a combined transliteration-and-meaning rendering that translates it as “Son of Sari.”

[He who wishes to study this profound prajna paramita Dharma gate, should contemplate in this way] The Song-dynasty translation of the Heart Sutra, the Buddha-Spoken Sutra of the Prajna Paramita of the Holy Mother of Buddhas, says:

“At that time, the bodhisattva mahasattva Avalokitesvara was in the Buddha’s assembly. This bodhisattva mahasattva, having been able to practice the profound prajna paramita, contemplated that the self-nature of the five aggregates is all empty. Then the venerable Sariputra, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, came forward and said to the bodhisattva mahasattva Avalokitesvara: If good men and good women, desiring to study this profound prajna paramita Dharma gate, should study it, how should they study? Then the bodhisattva mahasattva Avalokitesvara said to the venerable Sariputra: You should now listen attentively; I will proclaim it for you. If good men and good women desire to study this profound prajna paramita Dharma gate, they should contemplate the five aggregates: their self-nature is all empty.

What is meant by the self-nature of the five aggregates being empty? Namely, that form is emptiness, emptiness is form; form is not different from emptiness, emptiness is not different from form. Feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness are likewise so.
[Contemplation] Observing dharmas, both worldly and ultimate, with wisdom, and clearly illuminating and seeing them.

[Form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is not different from form; form is emptiness, emptiness is form] This means that the body of form is an illusory appearance, wholly identical with illusion (emptiness), because from the standpoint of essence all are nothing at all. The Buddha-Treasure Sutra says:
“The marks of all dharmas are all a single mark, namely the mark of no-mark.”
(Translation: The marks of all dharmas are all the same single mark, and this “mark” is: nothing.)

Generally speaking, “form” refers to all matter that has shape and occupies space, and this line of the sutra also applies to it—all matter that has shape and occupies space is an illusory appearance. But here the sutra is further clarifying “the five aggregates are all empty”; here “form” is the aggregate of form among the five aggregates, referring specifically to the body of form.

Question: “Form is not different from emptiness” is easy to understand, because the aggregate of form is illusory. But “emptiness is not different from form” is difficult to understand. Does it mean that all illusory appearances are the aggregate of form?

Answer: Form and emptiness are not different, and this is said from the standpoint of essence (ultimate reality). From the standpoint of the dream of ignorance, the aggregate of form is only a part of all marks, so all marks contain the aggregate of form but are not identical to it. But from the standpoint of the ultimate reality of all dharmas,
“the marks of all dharmas are all a single mark, namely the mark of no-mark.”
(The Buddha-Treasure Sutra.) Since they are all the single mark of being nothing at all, there is no question of one containing the other; rather, they are mutually identical (not two).
Question: How does one contemplate?

Answer: Prajna contemplation has two stages: understanding the principle (the meaning of the Middle Way, neither existence nor non-existence) and putting it into practice (the illusory-leaving practice of the dual operation of compassion and emptiness). Understanding the principle is the understanding, and putting it into practice is the practice. If prajna contemplation is to have real effect, understanding and practice must correspond: form understanding according to the principle, and initiate practice according to the understanding. Jiang Weinong’s Lectures on the Diamond Sutra says:
“In reading the sutras and hearing the Dharma, the point is to be deeply vigilant
(reverent caution)
, and to take what the Buddha said as a mirror, using it at all times and in all places to illuminate oneself
(to use it to check whether one’s body, speech, and mind accord with what the Buddha said; accord is awareness, discord is delusion)

. Without contemplating and illuminating, by what means does delusion recollect itself? This is what is meant by relying on the words to arouse contemplation. When contemplation has been practiced for a long time, then, grand and majestic
(the appearance of great splendor)

, the vigilant mind arises of itself—this is the beginning of awareness, the first opening of the right wisdom inherent in the principle-essence. Practicing thus without retreating or slackening, the work of contemplation deepens and matures day by day. Then what is called the beginning of awareness is first like a crescent moon, gradually more light and less darkness, until the orb of the moon is full and its radiance shines brightly, and the essence of the nature manifests. That is the beginning of awareness uniting with the original awareness, and with no longer any division between beginning and original. Know that what is called becoming a Buddha is nothing other than the complete illumination of the nature of awareness.”
The Elder Master Xuyun said:

“The Patriarch Bodhidharma said: ‘One who clearly understands the essential school of the Buddha-mind, and whose practice accords with his understanding, is called a patriarch.’ Practice according with understanding means, what you can say you can do.
Do not be turned by objects. It is like herding an ox: hold the rope firmly, and if the ox will not obey, give it a few lashes.
If you can always subdue your mind thus
, then in time, as the effort deepens, there will be news of reaching home.”
(From The Elder Xuyun’s Expedient Instructions.)
The Essentials of Mind Transmission says:

“This original pure mind is always of itself perfect, bright, and universally illuminating. People of the world do not awaken; they only take seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving as the mind, and are covered by seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving, so they do not behold the bright essential substance. But just directly set down the mind, and the substance appears of itself, like the great orb of the sun rising into empty space, universally illuminating the ten directions with no further obstruction. Therefore the student of the Way only takes seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving, and all activity and movement; empty out seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving, and the path of mind is cut off with no place to enter, but recognize the original mind right at seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving. Yet the original mind does not belong to seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving, nor is it apart from them. Only do not form views upon seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving, nor stir up thoughts upon them, nor seek the mind apart from them, nor grasp dharmas by abandoning them; not identical, not separate, neither abiding nor attached, free in all directions—nowhere is it not a place of practice.”

[Feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness are likewise so] This means that the mind is an illusory appearance—mental phenomena (feeling, thinking, conditioning, consciousness) are not different from illusion (emptiness). “Feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness are likewise so” is an abbreviated statement; stated in full it is: feeling is not different from emptiness, emptiness is not different from feeling, feeling is emptiness, emptiness is feeling; thinking is not different from emptiness, emptiness is not different from thinking, thinking is emptiness, emptiness is thinking; conditioning is not different from illusion, illusion is not different from conditioning, conditioning is illusion, illusion is conditioning; consciousness is not different from illusion, illusion is not different from consciousness, consciousness is illusion, illusion is consciousness.
This passage of the sutra further clarifies that body (form) and mind (feeling, thinking, conditioning, consciousness) are all illusory appearances.
The Smaller Prajna Paramita Sutra
Volume One says:

“Illusion is not different from form; form is not different from illusion; illusion is form, form is illusion; illusion is not different from feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness; consciousness is not different from illusion; illusion is consciousness, consciousness is illusion.”
The Great Prajna Paramita Sutra
Volume Forty-Two says:
“Form is not different from illusion; illusion is not different from form; form is illusion, illusion is form; feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness are likewise so.”
The Mahaprajnaparamita Sutra
Chapter Eleven, “The Study of Illusion,” says:
“Subhuti, what do you think? Is form different from illusion? Are feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness different from illusion? Subhuti replied: No, World-Honored One.”
From this we know that “emptiness” in the Heart Sutra is exactly “illusion.”

This passage of the sutra further clarifies the above-stated “illumines and sees that all five aggregates are empty.” “Form” is the mark of the body; everyone grasps it as self, and with a self there is “mine,” and so one sets oneself at the center and opposes oneself to other people, affairs, and things. This is the root of self-grasping, the hardest to break. Therefore, at the beginning of entering contemplation, one first contemplates that this body is a temporary combination of the four great elements, originally not existing, wholly empty in its very substance. If the self-nature is not imprisoned by this body, then birth and death, coming and going, are without any hindrance—this is called the breaking of the aggregate of form.

If the aggregate of form is broken, then the four aggregates of feeling, thinking, conditioning, and consciousness can be gradually contemplated deeply; for example: feeling is not different from emptiness, emptiness is not different from feeling, feeling is emptiness, emptiness is feeling; and so on, breaking them one by one.

In the Sutra of Complete Enlightenment, the bodhisattva Universal Eye requested the Buddha, for this assembly of bodhisattvas and for all sentient beings of the last age, to preach the gradual stages of bodhisattva practice: how should they think? How should they dwell and uphold? Since sentient beings have not awakened, what expedient means can universally bring them to awakening? The World-Honored One revealed:

“Good man! Those newly-learning bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the last age, who seek the Tathagata’s pure and perfect enlightened mind, should maintain right mindfulness and be far from all illusions. First, relying on the Tathagata’s practice of samatha, firmly uphold the precepts, peacefully house the assembly, and sit in meditation
(silently sitting in stillness)

in a quiet room, always thinking thus: This body of mine is a combination of the four great elements—so-called hair, fine hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, and the defiled color all return to earth; saliva, mucus, pus, blood, humors, spittle, phlegm, tears, essence and vital energy, and the excrement and urine all return to water; warmth returns to fire; movement returns to wind. When the four great elements each separate, where is this present false body? Then one knows that this body ultimately has no substance; being a combination it is a mark, and really is like an illusion. Through the temporary union of the four conditions, the six faculties falsely arise; the six faculties and the four great elements, combining within and without, falsely produce a breath of conditions that accumulates within; seeming to have a conditioned mark, it is provisionally called the mind. Good man! This false mind, if there were no six sense objects, could not exist. When the four great elements are dissolved, no sense object is to be obtained; within them the conditioned objects each return to dispersion and extinction, and ultimately there is no conditioned mind to be seen. Good man! For those sentient beings, because the illusory body is extinguished, the illusory mind is also extinguished; because the illusory mind is extinguished, the illusory objects are also extinguished; because the illusory objects are extinguished, the extinction of illusion is also extinguished; because the extinction of illusion is extinguished, that which is not illusion is not extinguished. It is like polishing a mirror: when the dust is exhausted, brightness appears. Good man! Know that body and mind are both illusory defilement; when the mark of defilement is forever extinguished, the ten directions are pure.”
